rewrites.summary:
Central Visayas holds the most active provincial-level anti-discrimination ordinance cluster outside the capital region: Mandaue City signed the Implementation Rules and Regulations of the Anti-Discrimination Ordinance in July 2024, formalised jointly with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and a UN development programme — an operational, not merely symbolic, local protection in the Cebu metro. The municipality of Carmen, northern Cebu, approved a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance protecting people on SOGIE grounds by unanimous Sangguniang Bayan vote in June 2025, days before the end of Pride month. A visitor in Cebu or Mandaue can invoke an operational anti-discrimination ordinance.

No killings, assaults or institutional-hostility incidents specific to trans visitors or residents are documented in this region within the 2024-2025 national violence series or elsewhere in the research record — protection without any accompanying regional violence signal.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Positioning context: the region holds the most active provincial-level anti-discrimination ordinance cluster outside the capital region — a comparative signal that the protections documented here are the exception rather than the rule among the regions of the country.
rewrites.localsOnly: The formalisation is resident-facing municipal administration: Mandaue City signed the implementation rules and regulations in July 2024 jointly with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and a UN development programme, and the municipality of Carmen passed its ordinance on a unanimous Sangguniang Bayan (municipal council) vote in June 2025 — the local governance machinery behind the protections a visitor could invoke.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No enforcement actions under either ordinance are documented in this record, so the operational protections are unverified in application. One municipal source was limited at fetch to the article header, leaving the exact enactment date beyond the research record's recoverable copy.

rewrites.summary:
In June 2025 a transgender-rights activist was shot dead in General Santos City. Human Rights Watch, an international human-rights organisation, called the killing an "apparent targeted killing" and said police were examining her activism as a possible motive; the national Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings of two transgender women as "marked by cruelty and impunity" and named her. The killing stood unresolved as of the record's sources, and no protective ordinance or institutional counterweight is documented in this region.

For a trans visitor the finding is targeted lethal violence against activists in a province with an official acknowledgement of impunity and no local machinery to answer it.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National framing: the national human-rights commission called the string of killings of transgender women a "disturbing pattern of transfemicide", the strongest official wording in this record for any region, and advocacy groups used the killings to push for a simplified legal gender-recognition bill — set against a national frame in which no national anti-discrimination statute exists and an equality bill has been pending in the legislature for 25 years.
rewrites.localsOnly: The victim was a resident activist figure in the region: she had served as deputy secretary general of a regional human-rights organisation in this region and as a journalist with a local broadcaster, and regional advocacy groups decried the killing — the local civil-society context in which the documented violence unfolded.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The killing stood unresolved as of the record's sources, with no prosecution or conviction status documented. Two source fetches were blocked (one record URL resolved to a rewritten, error-returning variant; one publisher blocks automated access), so portions of the source wording rest on the research dossier lines.

rewrites.summary:
The region's principal traveler-facing risk sits in Angeles City and the surrounding Clark-Subic corridor: in June 2025 the National Bureau of Investigation's Bataan District Office — the national investigative agency — dismantled a trafficking operation at a bar in Angeles City, arresting four people and rescuing 45 victims including 13 minors; in March 2025 the same office arrested a foreign national and accomplices in Angeles City under the expanded anti-trafficking in persons act, rescuing 12 victims including 5 minors.

For a transgender visitor the exposure is two-fold: the venues where trans women are concentrated in commercial sex work carry the highest violence and trafficking risk, and enforcement sweeps can sweep up anyone in the vicinity. No protective ordinance cluster comparable to the capital region or Central Visayas is documented here.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Comparative context: no protective ordinance cluster comparable to the capital region's or Central Visayas' is documented here, while regions with such clusters offer a local anti-discrimination recourse the record finds lacking in this region. National-framework context: national monitoring confirms traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas around the country, the frame under which the region's enforcement actions sit.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-side structural finding: peer-reviewed research describes the military-basing economy around the corridor as sustaining sexual markets that disproportionately exploit poor transgender Filipina women — the local population concentration behind the region's commercial-sex-work exposure.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No violence or trafficking incidents directly involving trans visitors inside the region's venues are documented in the research record, and the two-fold exposure is an inference from where trans women concentrate in commercial sex work. One structural source is dated 2019, and the national monitoring report's cached fetch returned only archive-page chrome, leaving some direct wording per the research dossier.

rewrites.summary:
This region surrounds the national capital, and the record documents no local protective ordinance here — so the visitor picture is the national one: killings of trans women without dependable local machinery.

Against that backdrop, in August 2025 an LGBTQ pageant winner who had just taken the title was found dead with 13 stab wounds in a city south of the capital, days after the win, and police worked the killing as a homicide case — a high-signal violent episode for this region's record.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National framework context: no national anti-discrimination law exists — an equality bill has been proposed since the 2000s and failed to pass, and in November 2022 the newly elected national government rejected international recommendations that included its passage — and transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender under the national regime. The country-overview source records murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming persons since at least 2012, the national frame in which this region's episode sits.
rewrites.localsOnly: The country-overview source lists local anti-discrimination ordinances inside this region — province-level and city-level enactments dating from the mid-2010s onward, including one later extended to cover gender identity — as resident-facing municipal protections not independently documented in this region's own record.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The record's statement that no protective ordinance is documented in this region and the overview source's list of ordinances inside the region are in tension, and no region-specific source in this record resolves the difference. The pageant-winner report identifies the victim's LGBTQ status but does not indicate transgender identity, so the episode's force as a trans-specific signal is unconfirmed. No disposition of the August 2025 homicide is documented.

rewrites.summary:
Two killings of trans women are documented in this region within the 2024-2025 national series. On 31 July 2024 in Ilagan City, Isabela, a 40-year-old trans woman was found dead in a cemetery after an alleged kidnapping and rape; three suspects were identified, and the monitored trans-murder count records the cause as stabbing. On 23 June 2025 the body of an 18-year-old trans woman student was found in a river in Cagayan province days after she was reported missing, with signs of physical assault noted; a young male student surrendered to police and denied involvement.

No protective ordinance, institutional-hostility finding or enforcement pattern specific to trans visitors is documented in this region beyond these incidents, so the visitor picture is violence without operative local protections.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Comparative national frame: the region's incidents sit in a documented national series — six killings of trans women in eighteen months tracked by a national monitoring project, with arrests made in at least three of them and none reported prosecuted to conviction. Advocacy and media responses renewed the call for an equality bill in a country where no national anti-discrimination statute has passed in 25 years, with groups citing the killings as proof that LGBTQ+ people remain unsafe.
rewrites.localsOnly: The second victim was a resident student at the regional state university and a hair-and-makeup artist active in local gay pageants — local community context for the 2025 killing. A criminology student of the regional university voluntarily surrendered to the local police, admitting he picked her up but denying involvement in the death.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The record's summary text describes the region's documentation as a single incident, while two of the attached source claims document a second trans-woman killing in the region (in Cagayan province, June 2025) — the discrepancy is unresolved in the research record, and the summarised text predates the second source set. None of the regional incidents is documented to a conviction.

rewrites.summary: No killings from the 2024-2025 national series occurred in this region, and the region's documented episode of institutional gender-expression policing was a campus directive applied to enrolled students, not a mechanism a visitor encounters. Its force as a visitor-relevant signal is indirect: in a conservative provincial setting, expression can be policed by institutional authority without an operational local recourse.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Region-to-region comparison: unlike the neighbouring Central Visayas record, this region has no protective ordinance cluster of comparable reach, so the documented episode sits against a region-to-region gap in available recourse.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The documented gender-expression policing (the 2022 Capiz State University directive) applied to enrolled students, not visitors.

On 10 October 2022 the university's Office of Student Affairs told students perceived as trans women that they would be barred from university premises unless they cut their hair and wore the uniform prescribed for males, delivering the instruction through campus guards with one week to comply and threatening that they could not re-enroll otherwise; the office attributed the order to the university president. A legal-NGO case study documents the students' subsequent advocacy campaign — backed by paralegals of national LGBTQ organisations, who pointed to an existing municipal anti-discrimination ordinance in Roxas City, Capiz province, which the office dismissed as inapplicable — and a later resident milestone: the first openly trans woman graduating as university valedictorian with highest honours, showing the policing reversed by advocacy.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the 2022 directive was formally withdrawn or remains formally in force is not documented; the record's reversal evidence is the later graduation milestone rather than a policy change. The Roxas City ordinance's existence is cited within the legal-NGO case study, but its current operative status is not independently documented in this record.

rewrites.summary:
A visitor in the Pangasinan corridor has a local complaint route absent in most other regions: Bayambang municipality's ordinance protecting the rights of LGBTQI persons on SOGIESC grounds — certified and affirmed at the provincial level in August 2024 — with complaints filed through the barangay mechanism under the local-government code, carrying a penalty ladder from fines to imprisonment.

The route is limited: the protection is municipal, and in the rural parts of two other provinces of the region a customary-justice system recognised by the national courts keeps its own dispute-resolution authority over defined offences, so the applicable institution in a dispute may not be a national court.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Comparative and scoring context: the record places the region's net effect marginally above the national score (+0.03) — modest because the protective ordinance is municipal and the alternative-justice uncertainty is localised to specific provinces within the region — and contrasts it with another region's record (Central Visayas, 0.63), where the ordinance cluster is broader (city implementation rules with institutional backing, unanimous municipal votes) and no countervailing alternative-justice structure exists.
rewrites.localsOnly: The municipal protection sits in provincial governance: the Pangasinan provincial board certified and affirmed the Bayambang ordinance by resolution in August 2024 — a provincial-level endorsement of a municipal ordinance in a conservative province. The region also hosts a codified customary-justice system (the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group) recognised by the national courts with its own dispute-resolution authority over the listed crimes and tribal-related offences — a resident-facing justice-pluralism structure operative in parts of two of the region's provinces.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific ruling or customary exclusion under the customary-justice system is documented in this record, so the alternative-justice uncertainty stays localised rather than demonstrated. The comparative scores cited here rest on the research record's own scoring, whose basis the attached sources do not restate; one attached source (the customary-justice journal item) was not retrievable at fetch time, and its currency status is unknown.

The resolution is a provincial-level endorsement giving LGBTQI persons a local legal complaint route in the corridor.

An official registry lists the ordinance, dated 16 October 2023, with a public page hosting the certified copy — confirming the number, series, author and enactment date the record cites.

rewrites.summary:
